Who moves where—and what housing choices do they make? uncovering spatial polarization through life-course migration in a shrinking megacity
abstract: Spatial polarization is a bottom-up process embedded in life-course trajectories rather than arising solely from macro-scale demographic decline. This study examines how life-course migration and housing choices shape spatial polarization in the Tokyo Metropolitan Area (TMA), a prototypical shrinking megacity. Using an integrated framework—combining survivorship-based cohort estimation, robust multiple linear regression, random forests, and geographically weighted regression—this research links micro-level residential decisions to broader demographic and structural transformations. Results identify three life-course migration cohorts whose divergent housing choices reinforce a polarized geography of youthful cores, family-oriented inner suburbs, and ageing peripheries. Young adults cluster in central Tokyo’s high-density rentals near transit hubs; young families pursue homeownership and educational access in western Tokyo and inner suburbs; while older seniors relocate to eastern Tokyo and peripheral municipalities, shaped by low-cost rentals and rural attachments. Across cohorts, housing tenure emerges as the strongest determinant of Migration Pattern Intensity (MPI), outweighing land prices, neighborhood characteristic, and accessibility. These findings advance the concept of a “polarized life-course housing trajectory” to explain how housing choices across life stages accumulate into multiscale polarization, intensified by intergenerational transfers. The study introduces this novel lens to bridge macro-structural shrinkage with micro-level residential practices to understand spatial polarization. Policy insights stress integrating foreign labor and multicultural inclusion at the regional scale and promoting multi-generational housing locally to mitigate suburban shrinkage and ageing. These strategies resonate with the SDGs and global sustainability agendas, offering lessons for urban governance in megacities confronting demographic contraction.

title: From human mobility to building functions: A deep learning approach for urban building classification in Megacity Tokyo
ML4EJ: Decoding the role of urban features in shaping environmental injustice using interpretable machine learning
abstract: Understanding the key factors shaping environmental hazard exposures and their associated environmental injustice issues is vital for formulating equitable policy measures. Traditional perspectives on environmental injustice have primarily focused on the socioeconomic dimensions, often overlooking the influence of heterogeneous urban characteristics. This limited view may obstruct a comprehensive understanding of the complex nature of environmental justice and its relationship with urban design features. To address this gap, this study introduces two primary contributions. First, this study develops an interpretable machine learning framework to examine the effects of various urban features, including the built environment, land cover, and human mobility, and socio-demographic and their non-linear interactions to the exposure disparities of three primary hazards: air pollution, urban heat, and flooding. The predictability performance of the models is used to measure the extent to which variations of urban features shape disparities in environmental hazard levels. Second, model transferability is used as a novel quantitative method to assess the similarity of these relationships across different regions and hazards, providing an empirical basis for understanding policy generalizability. Models were trained and tested with data from six metropolitan counties in the United States using Random Forest and XGBoost. The analysis of feature importance reveals features related to socio-demographic characteristics as the most prominent urban features that shape environmental hazard extent. Features related to transportation infrastructures and facility distribution are the relatively important urban features for urban heat exposure, and features related to land cover are the relatively important urban features for air pollution exposure, with significant variation across regions. The models show limited transferability across different regions and hazards, underscoring that the drivers of environmental injustice are context-specific. The insights gleaned from this study offer a fresh, data-driven perspective on the relationship among urban features and their interplay with environmental hazard exposure disparities, informing the development of more integrated urban design policies to enhance social equity and environmental injustice issues.

title: Street review: A participatory AI-based framework for assessing streetscape inclusivity
abstract: Urban centers undergo social, demographic, and cultural changes that shape public street use and require systematic evaluation of public spaces. This study presents Street Review, a mixed-methods approach that combines participatory research with AI-based analysis to assess streetscape inclusivity. In Montréal, Canada, 28 residents participated in semi-directed interviews and image evaluations, supported by the analysis of approximately 45,000 street-view images from Mapillary. The approach produced visual analytics, such as heatmaps, to correlate subjective user ratings with physical attributes like sidewalk, maintenance, greenery, and seating. Findings reveal variations in perceptions of inclusivity and accessibility across demographic groups, demonstrating that incorporating diverse user feedback can enhance machine learning models through careful data-labeling and co-production strategies. The Street Review framework offers a systematic method for urban planners and policy analysts to inform planning, policy development, and management of public streets. • Co-production and intersectionality are key to AI tools for inclusive urban analysis. • Sidewalk and building quality outweigh greenery in shaping perceived inclusivity. • Group evaluations provide nuanced and calibrated assessments of urban inclusivity. • Street Review combines ML, focus groups, and interviews for replicable urban analysis. • Demographic-specific heatmaps reveal inclusivity differences across user perspectives.

title: Foreign city users and in-store versus online retail channel choice: Urban logistics and planning implications
abstract: Abstract: This study examines the in-store and online purchasing behaviour of foreign city users (FCUs) in Bratislava, using a mixed-method quantitative approach that combines binary logit models with machine-learning classifiers, including support vector machines (SVM), random forests, and artificial neural networks. FCUs, defined as non-native residents such as international students, migrant workers, and refugees, display distinctive shopping patterns compared to locals, influenced by factors such as age, mobility resources, and product type. The analysis shows that FCUs are significantly less likely to shop online, particularly for essential goods, while younger FCUs are more inclined to purchase discretionary items online. The increased reliance of FCUs on physical retail for essentials tends to concentrate passenger trips in accessible districts (often walkable and transit-served, but in some contexts also around car-oriented shopping centres) whereas local higher uptake of online shopping generates more dispersed last-mile delivery flows. Beyond freight implications, this pattern helps policymakers calibrate the local retail mix and ensure its multi-modal accessibility (not only passenger trips). Policy recommendations include maintaining accessible retail in FCU-dense areas, improving multilingual e-commerce access, and strategically locating parcel collection infrastructure. The study underscores the need for demographic-sensitive retail and freight planning to support inclusive, sustainable, and resilient cities.

title: Rethinking urban shrinkage: An LLM-enhanced literature review of global landscapes and theoretical reconstruction of shrinking cities
abstract: As global urbanization enters the post-growth era, urban shrinkage has become increasingly prevalent, yet existing research often oversimplifies it as urban decline, overlooking the complexity and diversity of shrinkage processes. This study aims to systematically review global progress in shrinking cities research and reinterpret the essential characteristics and evolutionary patterns of urban shrinkage. The research employs a systematic literature review methodology, utilizing the ChatGPT-4o large language model to extract and analyze data from 183 articles, constructing an analytical framework across five dimensions: demographic-social, economic-industrial, spatial-land use, ecological-environmental, and governance-policy. The findings revealed: (1) Shrinking cities possess unique developmental logic, manifesting as complex evolutionary patterns where localized population return coexists with overall shrinkage; (2) Population flows demonstrate differentiated characteristics with out-migration of young, highly educated groups and retention of elderly, low-income populations, while some cities experience population decline coupled with sustained economic vitality; (3) Urban spatial restructuring manifests as simultaneous core decline and peripheral expansion instead of centripetal contraction alone, while abundant vacant land provides new opportunities for ecological restoration; (4) Future research should transcend simple binary frameworks, focusing on revealing the intrinsic mechanisms of localized revival, ecological equity, and multi-collaborative governance. This study unveils the knowledge structure and theoretical blind spots in shrinking cities research, providing evidence for developing more effective governance strategies for shrinking cities.

title: Impact of climate resilience policy on urban carbon intensity: Evidence from econometrics and machine learning
abstract: Urban carbon intensity (CI) is a key concern for improving climate conditions and promoting sustainable development. The climate resilient city pilot policy (CRCPP) implemented in China aims to actively address global climate change and foster sustainable development. The paper uses data from 278 Chinese cities between 2010 and 2021, employing the difference-in-differences model and machine learning to analyze the relationship between CRCPP and urban CI. The finding reveals that CRCPP effectively reduces urban CI. Meanwhile, the causal forest model, an advanced machine learning approach, corroborates this finding. Notably, the implementation of CRCPP in high economic development, high urbanization, and high CI cities is particularly effective in reducing CI. Concurrently, economic benefit analysis indicates that CRCPP not only lowers urban CI but also stimulates economic development. Furthermore, the policy synergistic effect of CRCPP when implemented in conjunction with energy saving and emission reduction fiscal policy enhances the effect of reducing urban CI. The outcomes of the paper offer useful insights for cities to formulate climate resilience plans and decrease urban CI.

title: Integrating AI and spatial analysis for resilient and inclusive 15-minute cities: A case study of Gdańsk
abstract: This study explores the application of artificial intelligence (AI) and geospatial tools to design 15-min cities, focusing on proximity, public space quality, environmental resilience, and inclusion. Using the post-industrial Young City district in Gdańsk, Poland, as a case study, the research integrates semantic segmentation (DeepLabv3) and AI-driven object detection for evaluating public space quality, flood simulation modeling (InVEST UFRM) for climate resilience, and network analysis using adjusted walking speeds (2.95 km/h) to capture the needs of vulnerable populations. By identifying “hotspots” with compounded deficits in access to urban amenities, public space quality, and resilience, the study provides a replicable, data-informed tool for guiding equitable urban transformation. The findings reveal critical spatial and environmental disparities, particularly in former fence-line neighborhoods in Gdańsk, which remain underserved despite ongoing urban redevelopment. The proposed framework offers practical insights for mainstreaming inclusive adaptation strategies into planning policies and contributes to the evolving discourse on operationalizing the 15-min city (FMC) concept in complex contexts.

title: Digital City, fewer emissions? Leveraging quasi-experiments to uncover big data's mediated climate impact
abstract: The development of big data provides substantial support for resource allocation and improves management efficiency; however, the effectiveness of the Big Data Strategy (BDS) in reducing Urban Energy Carbon Emission Intensity (UECEI) remains debated. This study employs a quasi-natural experiment, using China's National Big Data Comprehensive Pilot Zones as a policy shock. We apply a Difference-in-Differences (DID) model to analyze panel data from 278 Chinese cities between 2006 and 2021. The findings reveal that: (a) The BDS significantly reduces UECEI, a conclusion robust to Propensity Score Matching-DID (PSM-DID) tests, parallel trend tests, and other robustness checks; (b) Mechanism analysis confirms that artificial intelligence (AI) industry development and technological progress mediate this reduction. Urban entrepreneurial vitality, tertiary industry development, and government expenditure on science and education serve as positive moderators; and (c) Heterogeneity analysis indicates stronger policy effects in eastern regions, megacities, and traditional industrial cities. To enhance its emission-reduction potential, governments should tailor the BDS to regional contexts, foster cross-sector collaboration, invest in capacity building, implement impact monitoring, and encourage public participation.

title: Examining state-led gentrification using street view imagery: Evidence from Shanghai, China
abstract: This study introduces a transferable framework for detecting gentrification by leveraging detailed street-view imagery to capture visible changes in the built environment at the street level. The research utilizes deep learning techniques to analyze paired images from Shanghai spanning 2013 to 2022, allowing for the identification of neighborhood-level improvements. These visual findings are then systematically aligned with census data and case studies to strengthen the analysis. The approach proves especially effective within the context of state-orchestrated, property-led redevelopment, which is characterized by densification, public-space enhancement, and functional reconfiguration—hallmarks of entrepreneurial urbanism. The results reveal that such physical and functional upgrades are concentrated in central districts, waterfront corridors, and selected new towns, demonstrating that gentrification in Shanghai has gone beyond the traditional inner city, expanding to amenity-rich, brandable environments. The framework translates landscape transformations into consistent, citywide evidence, complementing conventional demographic and price-based measures. It offers spatiotemporally fine-grained monitoring and holds potential for application in other rapidly changing cities experiencing state-led gentrification.

title: Decoding mixed-use development in urban planning regulatory frameworks: A cross-national semantic analysis
abstract: This study decodes how mixed-use development, one of the most widely accepted yet variably operationalized principles in the pursuit of sustainable cities is framed in urban planning regulatory texts, across twelve cities, six countries and languages. The research brings to light how the notion of mixed-use or functional diversity is articulated, justified, and prioritized in diverse planning cultures. Through natural language processing NLP-based semantic analysis, the study identifies how mixed-use objectives are articulated and prioritized across planning cultures, synthesizing these framings into a structured comparative overview. Each rationale, be it economic, social, environmental, or morphological, is reflected with varying prominence across cases, revealing both convergence and divergence in how mixed-use is positioned within planning regulations of Los Angeles and Chicago (USA), São Paulo and Fortaleza (Brazil), Madrid and Zaragoza (Spain), Paris and Nantes (France), Jeddah and Dammam (Saudi Arabia), Shanghai and Shenzhen (China). Spatial coordination emerges as the shared regulatory core across all cases, while housing, service equity, economic activity, and regulatory flexibility objectives are selectively embedded, varying substantially across planning systems. The study deepens understanding of how mixed-use principles are conceptualized internationally at the level of regulatory language and illustrates the potential of AI to support systematic analysis of urban policy texts.

title: Measuring the level of circular economy in cities in alignment with sustainable development goal 11: Integration of machine learning algorithms and analytical hierarchical-network processes. A case study in Seville
abstract: The Circular Economy (CE) plays a crucial role in both transforming cities into inclusive, resilient, sustainable communities and addressing Sustainable Development Goal 11 (SDG11). However, current methods for the evaluation of city circularity are often incomplete due to their lack of multi-dimensional and comprehensive models and processes that encompass the three core pillars of sustainability, social, economic, and environmental, and SDG 11. This study addresses these limitations, by enabling precise hierarchical and network-based assessments and providing a quantitative score of city circularity. This hybrid model incorporates Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM) methods structurally inspired by Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) and Analytic Network Process (ANP), and Machine Learning (ML) models (pre-trained transformers, and Ensemble Learning (EL) techniques). The model operates across four levels: metrics, indicators, sustainability dimensions, and “circularity based on SDG11” (main goal) and measures their links. Semantic assessment and text mining analyze 123 metrics from 59 identified Circular City Indicators (CCIs). An ideal circularity score of 19.57 (equivalent to 100%) is calculated based on the maximum normalized values for all metrics. The proposed model is applied to the current data of Seville (Spain) in 2023, yields a circularity score of 7.25 (37.05%) under the proposed framework. The framework identifies key metrics with the highest impact on the final score while also recognizing secondary metrics with less influence on Seville's circularity score. This framework is a comprehensive tool for measuring city circularity, enabling cross-city comparisons and temporal analyses, while also being a powerful and adaptable instrument for different city levels, helping policymakers develop sustainable strategies.

title: Examining dual exposure to traffic congestion and in-vehicle crowding among senior and regular cardholders using smart card data
abstract: In urban travel, traffic congestion often results in prolonged travel times, while in-vehicle crowding causes physical discomfort. Bus passengers uniquely face dual exposure to both congestion (from shared road networks) and crowding (from shared vehicle space), which compounds health risks and undermines sustainable transport goals. Despite this, few studies examine these concurrent exposures or the socio-demographic disparities in who bears this burden, particularly critical for vulnerable populations like senior groups who may face disproportionate impacts. Using Beijing bus smart card data, we measure congestion and crowding levels to identify adverse travel patterns and infer passengers' home locations. We then apply statistical and random forest models to examine how socio-demographic characteristics shape exposure to these adverse conditions across different urban areas. The study reveals the spatial-temporal dynamics of congestion and crowding, the daily rhythms of adverse travel flow across urban spaces, and the socio-demographic characteristic disparities that shape differential exposures among senior and regular cardholders. The findings indicate that congestion concentrates in urban centers and suburban hubs during peak hours, while crowding tends to persist throughout the day on suburban-urban corridors. Urban residents experience more congestion but less crowding than suburban and rural residents. Senior cardholders experience shorter durations but higher rates of adverse conditions than regular cardholders. By revealing dual exposure patterns across space, time, and demographics, this study identifies where and when interventions are needed to reduce congestion for urban commuters and crowding for suburban riders.

title: A joint synthetic housing–household inventory
abstract: Accurately understanding the interactions between humans and the built environment requires integrated representations of both the buildings and the populations that occupy them. However, high-fidelity datasets that jointly capture detailed housing structures and demographic characteristics at the household level do not currently exist. This paper presents a framework for constructing a joint housing-household inventory that explicitly links individuals and households to compatible housing units from the National Structure Inventory (NSI), while preserving realistic population densities and demographic distributions. The framework integrates three components: (i) synthetic population generation from American Community Survey (ACS) Public Use Microdata Sample (PUMS) records that preserve complex intra-household relationships; (ii) a deep contrastive learning model that quantifies housing-household compatibility; and (iii) a hierarchical optimization-based allocation procedure that enforces building-level capacity and block-group-level demographic constraints. The generated synthetic population attains high statistical realism relative to the census microdata, and the contrastive learning model identifies compatible housing-household pairs with high predictive accuracy. Applied to coastal North Carolina, evaluations at building, neighborhood, and regional scales show that the joint inventory matches block-group-level demographic distributions, reproduces observed spatial population patterns without systematic bias, and maintains consistent allocation quality across urban, suburban, and rural contexts. By enabling coupled household- and building-level analyses, the resulting inventory supports a broad range of applications, including disaster resilience planning, housing and affordability analysis, energy-use assessment, and public health research.

title: Framing artificial intelligence as a policy instrument in urban climate action: Practitioners' perspectives from Paris
abstract: Urban practitioners increasingly integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into tasks related to the implementation of climate action. Research identified potential AI applications and traced implementation processes, yet it remains understudied how practitioners introduce AI and how AI systems change workflows and decision hierarchies in urban climate action. Treating AI as a policy instrument, this study examines the city of Paris through semi-structured interviews and documents from grey literature. We show that AI currently produces incremental shifts in tasks related to climate action, for example, in maintenance of infrastructure, urban planning and building regulation. These shifts in practice do not replace, but position urban practitioners as curators of AI systems, responsible for including socio-technical risk assessment and translation to deliberative formats. We also document how practitioners mediate AI’s integration into urban climate action through technocratic, moral, and political logics of action, contrasted with their doubts about the usefulness of AI. Doubts include, for instance, that AI risks depoliticizing urban climate action. By assessing AI as a socio-technical policy instrument rather than a neutral tool, our study unpacks both technical operational utility and its symbolic values, including tensions in between, such as complexity-handling versus oversimplification, and acceleration versus accountability. We argue that urban practitioners must critically reflect on their expectations towards AI systems and engage with fundamental concerns to reduce tension. Based on our findings, we created a checklist for urban practitioners who engage with AI in climate action and aim to operationalize democratic AI governance as a means to reduce adverse consequences.

title: Street characteristics and obesity: Evidence from Toronto and Greater Manchester using a scalable GeoAI framework
abstract: Obesity is increasingly recognised as being shaped by the built environment, yet evidence remains incomplete regarding how eye-level street characteristics relate to obesity across different urban contexts. This study examines how street-level environmental characteristics are associated with obesity prevalence and whether these relationships differ across urban contexts. Using Greater Manchester (UK) and Toronto (Canada) as comparative case studies, we develop a scalable geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI) framework that integrates Google Street View imagery, deep learning–based feature extraction, and machine-learning models. Objective street features and subjective perceptual attributes are analysed alongside neighbourhood-level environmental, socio-economic, and behavioural variables using Random Forest models with spatial block cross-validation and SHAP-based explainable AI. The results show that street-level characteristics contribute meaningfully to explaining spatial variation in obesity and exhibit pronounced non-linear and context-dependent associations. These findings highlight the importance of micro-scale street environments in urban health research and support more context-sensitive street-level planning interventions.

title: Data-driven bike-sharing rebalancing for smart cities: Reinforcement learning, operational constraints, and service-cost trade-offs
abstract: Dynamic bike-sharing rebalancing can improve bicycle availability, but its practical value depends on whether the service gains justify vehicle use and whether scarcity is merely transferred between locations. This study compares nine non-learned policies (no-op plus eight active comparators) with Maskable Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) in a full-network replay of the 2023 Warsaw station-based system. The analysis uses 2,994,604 recorded trips, 18,427,085 station-inventory observations, weather and spatial attributes for 310 physical stations, and a single modeled relocation vehicle with explicit travel, handling, depot, load, shift, route, and daily-resource constraints. Returns are always feasible; installed rack count is treated as infrastructure rather than as a hard inventory limit. Policies are evaluated over independent daily replays initialized from observed midnight states. The scientific configuration and five PPO checkpoint hashes were frozen before a 28-day November retrospective evaluation. No additional modeled rebalancing achieved a recorded-trip fulfilment rate (RTFR) of 99.036% with 1374 unfulfilled departures. Maskable PPO achieved 99.137% ± 0.011% and 1230.2 ± 16.0 failures, avoiding 143.8 failures (10.5%) relative to no-op; the paired moving-block interval for the failure difference was [−245.2, −56.6]. The myopic exhaustive analytical optimizer attained the highest RTFR (99.179%; 1171 failures) but used 1137.8 vehicle-km and 99.7 vehicle-hours, compared with 802.2 km and 60.0 h for PPO. PPO remained Pareto-efficient, but no active policy produced a positive modeled net benefit under three economic scenarios; the base-case PPO break-even value was 31.82 PLN per avoided failure. PPO improved 64 stations, worsened 33, and left 213 unchanged. These findings support selective, value-justified rebalancing rather than universal intervention or universal RL superiority.

title: Revisiting Gehl through perceived safety: A computational method
abstract: This study examines how ground-floor urban form relates to perceived safety in Stockholm, Sweden, using approximately one million street view images collected between 2010 and 2021 together with multi-source built-environment data. Jan Gehl’s writings discuss perceived safety as part of a human-centered design framework that integrates both traffic- and crime-related safety through street-level environmental design, drawing together ideas also established in broader planning and safety scholarship. Building on Gehl’s integrative framework, we operationalize a set of design attributes emphasized in his work and evaluate their associations with perceived safety scores derived from locally collected image-comparison surveys and extended citywide using deep learning models. Across multiple modeling approaches and two spatial scales, ground-floor features related to transparency and public–private transitions show the strongest and most consistent positive associations with perceived safety, often exceeding the explanatory strength of neighborhood demographic and land-use controls. Other features such as pedestrian and cycling infrastructure also demonstrate meaningful relationships, particularly at a finer spatial scale. These findings suggest that perceived safety is closely associated with the human-scale, street-level design features integrated within Gehl’s framework and demonstrate how computational urban analytics can operationalize qualitative design principles and evaluate their relevance to urban livability at scale.
